<noinclude><pagequality level="2" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader||SKY|203}}</noinclude> and the general law connecting the intensity of the scattered light with the wave-length follows almost as easily from considerations of ''dimensions.''

{{smaller block|The object is to compare the intensities of the incident and scattered light, for these will clearly be proportional. The number (<math>i</math>) expressing the ratio of the two amplitudes is a function of the following quantities:—(<math>\text{T}</math>) the volume of the disturbing particle; (<math>r</math>) the distance of the point under consideration from it; (<math>\lambda</math>) the wave-length; (<math>b</math>) the velocity of propagation of light; (<math>\text{D}</math>) and (<math>\text{D}'</math>) the original and altered densities: of which the first three depend only upon space, the fourth on space and time, while the fifth and sixth introduce the consideration of mass. Other elements of the problem there are none, except mere numbers and angles, which do not depend upon the fundamental measurements of space, time and mass. Since the ratio (<math>i</math>), whose expression we seek, is of no dimensions in mass, it follows at once that <math>\text{D}</math> and <math>\text{D}'</math> occur only under the form <math>\text{D} : \text{D}'</math>, which is a simple number and may therefore be disregarded. It remains to find how <math>i</math> varies with <math>\text{T}</math>, <math>r</math>, <math>\lambda</math>, <math>b</math>.}}

{{smaller block|Now, of these quantities, <math>b</math> is the only one depending on time; and therefore, as <math>i</math> is of no dimensions in time, <math>b</math> cannot occur in its expression. Moreover, since the same amount of energy is propagated across all spheres concentric with the particle, we recognize that <math>i</math> varies as <math>r</math>. It is equally evident that <math>i</math> varies as <math>\text{T}</math>, and therefore that it must be proportional to <math>\text{T}/\lambda r</math>, <math>\text{T}</math> being of three dimensions in space. In passing from one part of the spectrum to another, <math>\lambda</math> is the only quantity which varies, and we have the important law:—}}

{{smaller block|When light is scattered by particles which are very small compared with any of the wave-lengths, the ratio of the amplitudes of the vibrations of the scattered and incident lights varies inversely as the square of the wave-length, and the ratio of ''intensities'' as the inverse fourth power.}}

{{smaller block|The light scattered from small particles is of a much richer blue than the blue of the first order as reflected from a very thin plate. From the general theory (see {{sc|Interference of Light}}, § 8), or by the method of dimensions, it is easy to prove that in the latter case the intensity varies as <math>\lambda^{-2}</math>, instead of <math>\lambda^{-4}</math>.}}

{{smaller block|The principle of energy makes it clear that the light emitted laterally is not a new creation, but only diverted from the main stream. If <math>\text{I}</math> represent the intensity of the primary light after traversing a thickness <math>x</math> of the turbid medium, we have
{{block center|<math>d\text{I} = -h\text{I}\lambda^{-4}dx,</math>}}
where <math>h</math> is a constant independent of <math>\lambda</math>. On integration,
{{block center|<math>\log(\text{I}/\text{I}_0) = -h\lambda^{-4}x</math> . . . . . . (1)}}
if <math>\text{I}_0</math> correspond to <math>x=0</math>,—a law altogether similar to that of absorption, and showing how the light tends to become yellow and finally red as the thickness of the medium increases (''Phil. Mag.'', 1871, 41, pp. 107, 274).}}

{{smaller block|Sir William Abney has found that the above law agrees remarkably well with his observations on the transmission of light through water in which particles of mastic are suspended (''Proc. Roy. Soc.'', 1886).}}

{{smaller block|We may now investigate the mathematical expression for the disturbance propagated in any direction from a small particle upon which a beam of light strikes. Let the particle be at the origin of coordinates, and let the expression for the primary vibration be
{{block center|<math>\zeta = \sin(nt-kx)</math> . . . . . (2)}}
The acceleration of the element at the origin is <math>-n^2 \sin nt</math>; so that the force which would have to be applied to the parts where the density is <math>\text{D}'</math> (instead of <math>\text{D}</math>), in order that the waves might pass on undisturbed, is, per unit of volume,
{{block center|<math>(\text{D}'-\text{D})n^2 \sin nt.</math>}}
To obtain the total force which must be supposed to act, the factor <math>\text{T}</math> (representing the volume of the particle) must be introduced. The opposite of this, conceived to act at the origin, would give the same disturbance as is actually caused by the presence of the particle. Thus by equation (18) of § 11 of the article {{sc|Diffraction of Light}}, the secondary disturbance is expressed by
{{block center|<math>\zeta = \frac{\text{D}'-\text{D}}{\text{D}} \frac{n^2\text{T}\sin\phi \sin}{4\pi b^2} \frac{(nt-kr)}{r}</math>}}
{{block center|<math>= \frac{\text{D}'-\text{D}}{\text{D}} \frac{\pi\text{T}\sin\phi}{\lambda^2 r} \sin(nt-kr)</math> . . . . (3)<ref>In strictness the force must be supposed to act upon the medium in its actual condition, whereas in (18), previously cited, the medium is supposed to be absolutely uniform. It is not difficult to prove that (3) remains unaltered, when this circumstance is taken into account; and it is evident in any case that a correction would depend upon the square of <math>(\text{D}'-\text{D})</math>.</ref>}}}}
